title: Preferences for market justice in education: The role of meritocratic beliefs in the Chilean context
text:
Palabras clave: Market justice preferences; Education; Meritocratic beliefs; Chile; Latent profile analysis 

Abstract

title: 2  Introduction
text:
In recent decades, educational justice has emerged as a concept that has gained prominence in the study of educational inequalities. This trend has been driven by the expansion of market-based reforms in educational contexts and growing evidence of their harmful effects on equity (Camphuijsen et al., 2026; Francis et al., 2017; Sciffer et al., 2022). In the Chilean context, the commodification of education has led to the adoption of a “consumer-provider” logic, in which the educational system ends up mimicking market dynamics (Corvalán et al., 2016). These processes have consolidated an educational market that does not ensure equal access to opportunities, as financial barriers act as a prerequisite for enrollment in certain schools. Beyond that, the main problem is that, within this logic of competition, private schools offer a higher quality of education than public schools, a fact consistently demonstrated by national standardized tests (Bellei, 2025). These reforms do not merely entail changes in institutional architecture; they also implicitly alter the way people understand education. Thus, in a scenario where education operates under market forces, the concept of “market justice” becomes highly relevant for a deeper understanding of this process. As proposed by Lane (1986), “market justice” refers to the normative beliefs that legitimize the idea that access to and the quality of services—such as education—depend on the ability to pay (Lindh, 2015). Educational justice (as well as social justice) is at odds with market justice, since while the former seeks to level the playing field regarding background inequalities and guarantee equal opportunities regardless of social status, market justice defends educational inequality from the outset by limiting opportunities based on families’ purchasing power (Deutsch, 1975; Moyano, 2020; Walzer, 2010).
The justification for inequalities in education can be understood through classic self-interest hypotheses, in which people with higher status defend their social position by supporting the market or opposing redistribution. However, there are other factors that are equally important, if not more so, in this area, such as meritocracy. Known as a distributive system based on effort and talent (Young, 2017), meritocratic discourse attributes responsibility for success or failure to the individual. In the educational context, meritocracy lies at the heart of every educational institution, where it is presented as an ideal, promising that those who work the hardest will receive rewards commensurate with their efforts (Darnon et al., 2018). However, outcomes are influenced by students’ family backgrounds and, more broadly, by the structural conditions of society. The meritocratic narrative overlooks the role of underlying conditions in people’s educational trajectories, thereby functioning as a mechanism for legitimizing inequality, since individuals are held responsible for their outcomes—whether success or failure (Clycq et al., 2014; Mijs, 2016).
Until now, the literature has studied meritocracy with a particular focus on perceptions of effort and talent, but I argue that examining the relationship between market justice in education and meritocracy requires a broader model than one based solely on perceptions of merit. In this regard, Castillo et al. (2023) proposed a conceptual framework that makes two distinctions: First, it distinguishes between perceptions and preferences. Perceptions refer to how people observe meritocracy operating in society, while preferences refer to how society should operate. Second, it distinguishes between meritocratic beliefs—which are related to effort and talent—and privilege beliefs, which are expressed through family background and social connections. Thus, the framework encompasses both perceptions and preferences regarding beliefs about meritocracy and privilege. Based on this multidimensional framework of meritocracy, evidence supports the view that meritocratic beliefs and privilege beliefs are neither opposites nor part of the same continuum, but rather distinct dimensions and can therefore coexist in people’s minds (Castillo et al., 2023).
Previous studies have examined the relationship between market justice and meritocracy finding positive asociations, but without a multidimensional framework to observe how meritocratic beliefs operate alongside those based on privilege (Castillo et al., 2024; Castillo, Laffert, et al., 2025; Castillo et al., 2026). Similarly, most studies examining market justice and meritocracy have relied on variable-centered methods, which make it impossible to determine whether beliefs are heterogeneous within the population (Castillo, Laffert, et al., 2025; Castillo et al., 2026). This research aims to contribute to the agenda of meritocracy and market justice in two ways: First, I apply a novel person-centered approach, which assumes not everyone shares the same beliefs, allowing us to identify patterns of belief based on shared attributes—an approach that is uncommon in sociological studies (Van Hootegem, 2022; Zhu, 2025). This makes possible to observe how meritocratic and privilege-related beliefs are organized in people’s minds in terms of the number and size of groups. Furthermore, I am seeking to understand how each group relates to market justice in education, hoping to discover new perspectives by studying the diversity of beliefs about merit alongside privilege. The latest contribution aims to demonstrate that there is a complex interplay between meritocracy and the legitimacy of inequalities that is not straightforward.
Based on the literature, the main argument is that where merit-based beliefs predominate, their relationship with market justice in education will be positive, reinforcing the narrative of meritocracy as a legitimizer of inequalities. Thus, the two research questions underlying this study are: (1) How do meritocratic and privilege belief patterns manifest themselves in terms of the number of identifiable groups and their size? (2) How do different groups of people, based on meritocratic and privilege-based beliefs, relate to market justice in education?
This study is particularly relevant in Chile, a country characterized by high levels of inequality and a system in which social goods are highly commodified (Boccardo, 2020; Castillo, Iturra, et al., 2025). The neoliberal reforms of the civil-military dictatorship (1973–1989) have produced structurally segmented systems in health care, pensions, and education, in which access and quality depend on ability to pay, benefiting higher-income sectors and relegating the poorest to limited, underfunded public alternatives (Madariaga, 2020). Specifically, the education system is highlighted as one of the most privatized in the world, where the quality of private education surpasses that of public education due to limited regulation of the education market, as reflected in high levels of school segregation and low regard for public education (Bellei, 2016, 2025; Ramos, 2022; Valenzuela et al., 2014). To address these issues, a series of policies have been developed in recent years with the goal of reducing school segregation and lowering barriers in access to education (Bellei & Munoz, 2023). Despite this, people continue to hold strong meritocratic beliefs, illustrating the inequality paradox (Mijs, 2021; PNUD, 2017). Thus, in a context marked by high and durable inequalities, deep marketization of education, and the entrenchment of meritocratic beliefs, it is relevant to examine the link between meritocratic beliefs and market-justice preferences in education.

title: 3  Theoretical and empirical background
text:
3.1 Market justice preferences
Research on distributive justice has gradually incorporated market preferences into attitudinal research on redistribution. Since Kluegel’s seminal work (1981) on the normative foundations of beliefs about social stratification, the concept of market justice preferences —coined by Lane (1986)— has been developed, understood as the normative principle that legitimizes access to goods and services according to an individual’s or family’s ability to pay (Lindh, 2015). In this regard, market is considered fair because the payment capacity of individuals is interpreted as responsive to effort, where the outcomes are concived as earned deserts (J. R. Kluegel et al., 1999; Lane, 1986). This principle is closely linked to the justification of inequalities: by conceiving the market as a space of equal opportunities, economic success is interpreted as an individual achievement (J. R. Kluegel et al., 1999), disregarding the structural conditions that produce such disparities. In this way, market justice operates simultaneously as an economic and moral principle that legitimizes socioeconomic inequalities.
In recent years, education has become one of the key dimensions in the study of market justice. The introduction of market logic into educational institutions has largely led to the loss of education’s intrinsic value in its commitment to equal opportunity, with the generation of monetary value taking precedence over everything else (Abowitz & Stitzlein, 2018; Ball, 2004; Brancaleone & O’Brien, 2011; Piketty & Sandel, 2025; Satz, 2010). In the Chilean context, the market has come to be seen as an inseparable element of education, to the point where it is referred to as the “education market” rather than education itself (Corvalán et al., 2016). The education market has been sustained over the past 50 years by the neoliberal policies implemented during the dictatorship (1973–1989), which have established the predominance of private institutions over public ones in terms of educational quality, leading to a proliferation of educational inequalities in areas such as student outcomes, school segregation, and school infrastructure, to name a few (Bellei, 2016, 2025; Canales et al., 2016; Ramos, 2022; Valenzuela et al., 2014). Consequently, the education market—where the quality of and access to education depend on how much money families have—does not allow educational opportunities to be distributed fairly.
Most research in the market justice field relies on survey data, in which questions directly probe support for the provision of social services—education, pensions, and health care—based on individual ability to pay (e.g., “Is it fair that high-income individuals receive better education than low-income individuals?”) (Busemeyer, 2013; Lindh, 2015). Within this framework, International Social Survey Programm (ISSP) has been the primary source for advancing this agenda,but considering only education and health care items. Also, recent chilean research have added a item refered to pensions and employed a separate analysis of each item (education, health care and pensions) (Castillo, Iturra, et al., 2025; Castillo et al., 2026), but also have been implemented indexes constructed from relevant items (Castillo, Laffert, et al., 2025).
Recent literature on market preferences has identified significant associations mainly at individual level. Socioeconomic status emerges as a consistent predictor; those in more advantaged positions tend to exhibit greater preferences for market justice (Koos & Sachweh, 2019; Lindh, 2015), a pattern reflecting a moral economy that justifies status for those who benefit from the market order. In this regard, political ideology shows a clear association, with right-leaning individuals tending to favor market-oriented distributional principles (Castillo et al., 2024; Lee & Stacey, 2024). Along the same lines, meritocracy has emerged as another important factor associated with market justice, where the meritocratic narrative has been positively correlated with pro-market positions (Castillo et al., 2024; Castillo, Iturra, et al., 2025; Castillo et al., 2026; Heuer et al., 2020). In this research, I focus in the individual level factors related to market justice in education, specially on meritocracy as a catalyst for justifying inequalities.

title: 3  Theoretical and empirical background
text:
3.2 Meritocratic beliefs
When discussing education, it is difficult not to encounter the concept of meritocracy. Based on Michael Young’s work The Rise of Meritocracy (1962) (2017), this concept is understood as the distribution of rewards based on effort and talent. For their part, schools award credentials that reflect students’ performance in various subjects. In this sense, meritocracy is a fundamental element of every educational institution, as it is one of the principles governing the awarding of credentials. Thus, beliefs about the educational system are often closely tied to meritocracy (Clycq et al., 2014; Darnon et al., 2018).
In the field of education, meritocracy has been used as a distributive principle, but within this framework, it has also been linked to the justification of inequalities. Starting from Adams’ theory of equity (1963), meritocracy operates as a universal equality principle, where rewards should be commensurate with effort. Several studies have shown that meritocratic beliefs are associated with individualistic beliefs, such as an aversion to redistribution and a preference for market justice (Bartram, 2023; Castillo et al., 2024; Castillo, Iturra, et al., 2025; Mijs, 2021; Sin et al., 2026), and are characteristic of those in more privileged social positions (Heuer et al., 2020). In these cases, meritocracy is used to legitimize positions, with those who benefit from the system often justifying their success on the basis of their own merit, overlooking the structural conditions that shape reality. Thus, the merit narrative is linked to support the idea that money should determine the quality and access to education. This normative judgment runs counter to educational justice, as it hinders equal opportunities and, ultimately, determines students’ educational trajectories (Moyano, 2020; Walzer, 2010).
In the meritocracy research framework, most studies have used surveys to respond their research questions, with the International Social Survey Program as the main instrument for measuring and analyzing meritocratic beliefs in both national and international contexts. These items show the relevance of meritocratic and privilege factors for getting ahead in life, like effort and contacts, respectively. Following this conceptual model, there is a tradition of studying meritocratic beliefs from a unidimensional perspective (García-Sánchez et al., 2019; Mijs, 2021). The problem with this approach is that it has serious implications for understanding social reality, since it assumes that people’s beliefs follow a rational logic in which, if a belief in meritocracy is stronger, a belief in privilege must be weaker. To address this, in recent years, some authors have proposed a multidimensional perspective on meritocracy, constructing frameworks that allow for distinguishing the dimension of merit from that of privilege, on the one hand, and differentiating perceptions from preferences on the other (Castillo et al., 2023; Duru-Bellat & Tenret, 2012; Zhu, 2025). These advances have led to two key contributions: (1) to capture the coexistence of beliefs that may be considered contradictory and, consequently, (2) to demonstrate that people can hold different sets of meritocratic beliefs.
While the multidimensional perspective on meritocracy allows for a more detailed examination of people’s beliefs, a caveat remains about the individuals who hold them. So far, we do not know how different combinations of these dimensions operate in people’s minds or how prevalent they are in populations. Several methods have addressed these issues by estimating how variables can group into persons, with Latent Class Analysis (LCA) among the most promising approaches. LCA is a person-centered approach that allows us to identify the heterogeneity of individuals’ beliefs by clustering them, going beyond the scope of variable-centered methods, which assume that the association between two or more variables in the population behaves uniformly (Cech & Blair-Loy, 2010). In our context, one advantage of this approach is that it accommodates the possibility that individuals may hold both meritocratic and structuralist beliefs, allowing for a theoretical and methodological examination of multidimensional meritocracy (Nylund-Gibson & Choi, 2018; Zhu, 2025).
Although LCA allows us to identify different configurations of meritocratic beliefs, it is not possible to define in advance the types of patterns that will be found. In this regard, the evidence suggests that one of the most likely patterns is a predominant meritocratic beliefs, in which individuals consider merit important and structural factors unimportant (Heuer et al., 2020; Xian & Reynolds, 2017; Zhu, 2025). On the other hand, a pattern has also been identified in which success is attributed to family and background conditions rather than effort (C. Palomino & Sebastian, 2026). Finally, a pattern of dual consciousness has been identified, in which individuals consider merit, family connections, and wealth to be important (Zhu, 2025). Therefore, based on previous studies, this research expect to find at least three types of groups based on meritocratic beliefs: a meritocratic-dominant latent class viewing merits as important while deeming privilege factors as irrelevant; a class characterized by aware of privilege, viewing privilege factors as important while deeming merits as unimportant, and finally a dual consciousness class, viewing merits and privilege factors as important simultaneously.
Each pattern of meritocratic beliefs can be situated within a framework of meaning related to a preference for market justice in education. As the literature suggests, the perception of meritocracy is widely associated with the legitimization of inequalities—and specifically with market justice—so it is to be expected that the first group would adhere to this pattern (Castillo, Laffert, et al., 2025; Castillo, Iturra, et al., 2025). With regard to the second group, the prevalence of privilege could be directly associated with disagreement over education-market justice preferences, since observing that society distributes rewards based on factors unrelated to merit might seem unfair (Alesina & La Ferrara, 2005). Finally, the pattern of dual consciousness may demonstrate that the recognition of merit and privilege in the functioning of society could imply an understanding that structural conditions play an important role in individual outcomes, leading to opposition to the idea that access to and the quality of a service such as education should be based on economic conditions (Xian & Reynolds, 2017; Zhu, 2025). Based on the above, the following hypotheses emerge:
\(H_{1}\): Predominant meritocratic beliefs class shows a positive association with education market justice preferences
\(H_{2}\): Aware of privilege beliefs class shows a negative association with education market justice preferences
\(H_{3}\): Dual consciousness beliefs class shows a negative association with education market justice preferences

title: 3  Theoretical and empirical background
text:
3.3 Associated factors
There are various theories regarding how educational attainment affects people’s redistributive preferences. On the one hand, there are theories that view education as a resource that enhances the development of technical skills and/or critical thinking, leading individuals to become aware of structural problems and, as a result, to support the reduction of inequality (Becker, 1993; Freire, 2015; Schultz, 1961). On the other hand, in cultural reproduction theories, education has been understood as a source of social inequalities, as it reproduces individuals’ living conditions, preventing opportunities for intergenerational social mobility and, consequently, perpetuating the stratified social order (Bourdieu, 2019; Bowles & Gintis, 2011). Within the framework of redistributive preferences, reproductionist notions are grounded in self-interest theory, whereby those with higher levels of education tend to exhibit attitudes that reflect a desire to protect their privileged social positions, which could be understood as an aversion to redistribution or support for market-based justice. Thus, education can be understood not only as an enlightening force in social life but also as a cog in the reproduction of inequalities.
Recent literature provides empirical support for these two theoretical approaches to education. For example, research by Nye et al. (2026) found, in an analysis of 282 country-year combinations from various international surveys, that in 95% of cases, education was positively associated with market-oriented attitudes. Likewise, Van Noord et al. (2019) used data from 31 countries to show that education is widely understood as the basis for social stratification. Other studies have found that higher levels of education are associated with a greater preference for public investment (Busemeyer, 2012) However, the results from Liu & Wang (2026) suggest that education does not fulfill a generalized function; rather, both the enlightening and the reproductionist roles exist but depend on the level of education, where in countries with low inequality, basic education is associated with reproductionist positions, while in secondary and tertiary education, the enlightening role stands out.
Given the important role that education plays in shaping individuals’ attitudes toward inequality, this study proposes the following hypothesis:
\(H_{5}\): Individuals with higher levels of education show higher education market justice preferences
In addition to educational level, the literature has shown that income is also an important factor in the study of attitudes toward inequality (Heuer et al., 2020; Lindh, 2015). The evidence shows that higher-income individuals tend to support market-based distributive principles (Immergut & Schneider, 2020; Lindh, 2015; Nye et al., 2026). In this context, among higher-status social groups, there is congruence between their attitudes and their individual outcomes—that is, a legitimization of the market as a distributor of rewards, serving as a justification for social status. Although the link between income and market justice can be tied to self-interest theories, Langsæther & Evans (2020) argues that social status does not always provide a rational explanation for attitudes toward inequality, making it necessary to test this relationship. Based on the literature, the corresponding hypothesis is:
\(H_{6}\): Individuals with higher incomes show higher education market justice preferences
Political ideology also influences people’s attitudes toward inequality. In this regard, the scientific literature has shown that people with right-wing political ideologies tend to support a market-based distribution of welfare (Lee & Stacey, 2024). Meanwhile, (Van Hootegem, 2022) found that right-wing individuals are less likely to adopt positions that support equity and equality. This finding is consistent with the study by Castillo, Iturra, et al. (2025), which found that only individuals identifying with right-wing ideologies showed a positive correlation with a preference for market justice in education. In this context, the following hypothesis is proposed:
\(H_{7}\): Right-wing individuals show higher education market justice preferences than those belonging to the left-wing
Finally, I examine the moderating role of education in the relationship between meritocratic belief patterns and preferences for education market justice. Given that education can play either an enlightenment or a reproductionist role, it would be interesting to observe how educational level can amplify or attenuate the relationship between each latent class and education market justice preferences. Since I do not have sufficient evidence to support this hypothesis, this analysis is exploratory. Thus, the following hypothesis emerges:
\(H_{8}\): Classes that are positively associated with education market justice preferences show an amplified effect when moderated by educational level

title: 3  Theoretical and empirical background
text:
3.4 This study
This study argues that implementing a private social services architecture has consequences for the population’s normative judgments, with meritocracy emerging as a driving force shaping people’s conceptions of justice in the educational sphere. Meritocracy has been used as a narrative to define success and failure in terms of individual responsibility, especially in educational institutions where meritocracy plays a central role, so considering that, I argue that meritocratic alongside privilege beliefs provide a key normative lens through which individuals evaluate education inequalities. Based on this argument, this research aims to further explore the research area of market justice and meritocracy through two innovations: First, the identification of different belief systems in Chile using a multidimensional framework of meritocracy and privilege, combined with a person-centered method, distinguishing the heterogeneity of beliefs in terms of the size and number of recognizable systems. Second, to explore how each belief system relates to preferences for market justice preferences in education. Thus, this study aims to demonstrate that meritocracy can function differently as a mechanism for legitimizing inequalities in education, and that this difference in its functioning as a mechanism can only be observed by acknowledging the heterogeneity of beliefs within the population. The hypotheses proposed in this study are the follows:
\(H_{1}\): Individuals with higher levels of education show higher education market justice preferences
\(H_{2}\): Individuals with higher incomes show higher education market justice preferences
\(H_{3}\): Right-wing individuals show higher education market justice preferences than those belonging to the left-wing
In light of the foregoing, it is worth analyzing this phenomenon in Chile, a country that offers an interesting case for examining how public attitudes toward the distribution of social services are affected by market-oriented welfare institutions. Chile is one of the most unequal countries in the OECD, with a high concentration of income and wealth in the top decile (Chancel et al., 2026; Flores et al., 2020). This inequality is largely attributable to the neoliberal reforms of the civil-military dictatorship, subsequently expanded by democratic governments, which privatized and commodified key spheres of social reproduction through concessions and regulatory frameworks favorable to private provision (Madariaga, 2020; PNUD, 2017). This model has produced structurally segmented systems in health care, education, and pensions, where access and quality depend on the ability to pay, benefiting higher-income sectors and relegating the poorest to limited, underfunded public alternatives (Boccardo, 2020; Castillo, Laffert, et al., 2025). In detail, the education system is characterized as one of the most privatized in the world, where the quality of private education surpasses that of public education due to the limited regulation of the education market, and where high levels of private-sector investment coexist with a lack of public funding (Bellei, 2025; Ramos, 2022; Valenzuela et al., 2014). Thus, in a context marked by high and durable inequalities, a well-established education market, and the entrenchment of meritocratic beliefs, it becomes relevant to examine the link between meritocratic beliefs and preferences for education market justice (Castillo, Laffert, et al., 2025). Ultimately, this research aims to explain how market-based normative beliefs may prevent educational institutions from ensuring equal opportunities, thereby bringing educational justice to the forefront of public discussion.

title: 4  Data, Variables and Methods
text:
4.1 Data
The data come from the EDUMERCO dataset, a survey conducted as part of the EDUMER-funded project that focused on beliefs and attitudes toward meritocracy and inequality. The survey was conducted in 2025 via Computer-Assisted Web Interviewing (CAWI) among adults aged 18 to 75 in the Santiago Metropolitan Region of Chile. The sampling design was a quota-based non-probability sample, with quotas for age, sex, educational level, and socioeconomic status that approximated the population parameters. The total sample consisted of 3,470 respondents, while the analytical sample consisted of 2,489 respondents.

title: 4  Data, Variables and Methods
text:
4.2 Variables
The dependent variable of this study is the preference for market justice in education. This construct is measured using the following statement: “It is just that high-income people have a better education for their children than people with lower incomes” (“Es justo que las personas de altos ingresos tengan una mejor educación para sus hijos que las personas con ingresos más bajos” in Spanish). The response categories are on a four-point Likert scale from (1) “strongly disagree” to (4) “strongly agree”.
The main independent variable in this study is meritocratic beliefs. To this end, two areas are distinguished: (1) meritocratic perceptions and preferences, and (2) perceptions and acceptance of privilege. Meritocratic and privilege-based perceptions and preferences were measured using the same items proposed in the original scale (Castillo et al., 2023). The dimensions are summarized in Table 4.1.

Each item is rated on a four-point Likert scale ranging from “strongly disagree” (1) to “strongly agree” (4), higher scores indicate stronger endorsement of the corresponding perception or preference.
In addition, other independent variables considered are educational level, income and political identification. Educational level is measured using the question: “What is the most recent course or level of study you completed?”. The response categories range from 1 to 9, where higher values indicate a higher level of education among respondents. This variable was subsequently dichotomized to examine differences between individuals with and without higher education. Income was measured using a question asking about the person’s monthly income, with 10 response categories. For modeling purposes, this variable was recategorized into 5 categories, expressed as quintiles. Finally, political identification is measured along a left-right axis using a 6-category scale, where 1 indicates right, 5 indicates left, and 6 indicates independent. title: 4  Data, Variables and Methods
text:
4.3 Analytical strategy
The analysis proceeds in three steps. First, a latent profile analysis (LPA) identifies subgroups of respondents that share a common configuration of meritocratic perceptions and preferences. Second, each respondent is assigned to the profile to which they most likely belong. Third, an ordinal logistic regression estimates the association between profile membership and the preference for market justice in education, net of sociodemographic and political controls.

4.3.1 Latent profile analysis
LPA is a person-centered finite mixture model. It assumes that a population that looks homogeneous is in fact a mixture of a small number of unobserved subgroups, and it uses the pattern of responses to a set of indicators to estimate each respondent’s probability of belonging to each subgroup (Jason & Glenwick, 2015). This fits the aim of the study, which is not to place respondents on a single meritocracy scale but to uncover qualitatively different combinations of perceptions and preferences, such as endorsing meritocracy while also perceiving or accepting privilege. LPA and latent class analysis (LCA) are very similar and share the same fit statistics. They differ in the type of indicator: LCA is designed for categorical indicators and describes classes by conditional probabilities of endorsement, whereas LPA is used for continuous indicators and describes profiles by their mean on each indicator (Jason & Glenwick, 2015; Scotto Rosato & Baer, 2012). The eight items are four-point Likert responses. LPA is used because they are treated as continuous, which retains the intensity of agreement that dichotomizing the items for an LCA would discard. Treating ordinal items with four categories as continuous is a common simplification, but it is an assumption and a limitation of this specification.
Solutions with one to five profiles are estimated in R with the tidyLPA package, using maximum likelihood estimated through the Expectation-Maximization algorithm and random starting values, with a fixed seed for reproducibility. The number of profiles is chosen by combining statistical and substantive criteria, since no single index is decisive:

Information criteria. AIC and BIC are compared across solutions, with lower values indicating better fit. BIC has been identified as the most reliable index for selecting the number of classes. Because these indices tend to keep decreasing as profiles are added, the size of each improvement relative to the K−1 solution is examined, and a marginal gain suggests that an extra profile adds little.
Classification quality. Relative entropy (0 to 1) assesses how clearly respondents are separated into profiles, with higher values indicating more accurate classification. After selecting the solution, the mean posterior probability of the assigned profile is reported for each profile.
Profile size. The proportion of the smallest profile is examined, and solutions with very small profiles are viewed with caution because they tend to be unstable.
Interpretability. The final decision depends on whether the profiles make theoretical sense and differ qualitatively, not only quantitatively, in their pattern of means.

A class or profile is a statistical construct, not necessarily a real group. Spurious profiles can arise from non-normality or from misspecification of the model, so the profiles are interpreted as useful descriptions of belief configurations and not as proof of tangible subgroups.


4.3.2 Ordinal logistic regression
After selecting the number of profiles, each respondent is assigned to the profile with the highest posterior probability (modal assignment). Preference for market justice in education, a five-category ordered response, is then regressed on profile membership with ordinal (proportional-odds) logistic regression, estimated with the MASS package in R. Results are reported as odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and the reference category is the Partial meritocrats profile.
Seven models are estimated. Model 1 includes only profile membership. Model 2 adds sex, university education and income quintile, and Model 3 adds political identification. Models 4 to 6 add to Model 3 the interaction of profile with each political category (left, center and right, respectively, with those who do not identify with any position as reference), and Model 7 adds the interaction of profile with university education. The interactions examine whether the association between profile and the outcome varies across these groups. Each political interaction is estimated in a separate model so that their effects do not overlap.
Modal assignment treats profile membership as known, although it is estimated with error, which tends to attenuate the association with the outcome. The mean posterior probability of each profile is reported as an indicator of how large this uncertainty is.


4.3.3 Robustness analysis
to prevent latent profiles from being an artifice due to suspicious response patterns, Respondents flagged as careless responders were excluded before estimation. Three indices were computed on the eight items (longstring, intra-individual response variability and Mahalanobis distance), and respondents flagged by at least two of them were removed, as were those with missing values on any indicator (Curran, 2016; Ward & Meade, 2023). The resulting sample is far above the minimum of about 100 cases usually recommended for mixture models.

title: 3  Theoretical and empirical background
text:
3.3 Estatus, political ideology and moderation

3.3.1 Education
There are various theories regarding how educational attainment affects people’s redistributive preferences. On the one hand, there are theories that view education as a resource that enhances the development of technical skills and/or critical thinking, leading individuals to become aware of structural problems and, as a result, to support the reduction of inequality (Becker, 1993; Freire, 2015; Schultz, 1961). On the other hand, in cultural reproduction theories, education has been understood as a source of social inequalities, as it reproduces individuals’ living conditions, preventing opportunities for intergenerational social mobility and, consequently, perpetuating the stratified social order (Bourdieu, 2019; Bowles & Gintis, 2011). Within the framework of redistributive preferences, reproductionist notions are grounded in self-interest theory, whereby those with higher levels of education tend to exhibit attitudes that reflect a desire to protect their privileged social positions, which could be understood as an aversion to redistribution or support for market-based justice. Thus, education can be understood not only as an enlightening force in social life but also as a cog in the reproduction of inequalities.
Recent literature provides empirical support for both reproductionist and enlightenment approaches to education. In support of the reproductionist approach, research by Nye et al. (2026) found, in an analysis of 282 country-year combinations from various international surveys, that in 95% of cases, individual educational level was positively associated with market-oriented attitudes. Likewise, Van Noord et al. (2019) used data from 31 countries to show that education is widely understood as the basis for social stratification. In support of the enlightenment approach, Busemeyer (2012) found that higher levels of education are associated with a greater preference for public investment. However, the results from Liu & Wang (2026) suggest that education does not fulfill a generalized function; rather, both the enlightening and the reproductionist roles coexist but depend on the level of education. In countries with low inequality, basic education is associated with reproductionist positions, while secondary and tertiary education highlight the enlightening role.
Given the important role that education plays in shaping individuals’ attitudes toward inequality, this study proposes the following hypothesis:
\(H_{4}\): Individuals with higher levels of education show higher education market justice preferences


3.3.2 Income
In addition to educational level, the literature has shown that income is also an important factor in the study of attitudes toward inequality (Heuer et al., 2020; Lindh, 2015). The evidence shows that higher-income individuals tend to support market-based distributive principles (Immergut & Schneider, 2020; Lindh, 2015; Nye et al., 2026). In this context, among higher-status social groups, there is congruence between their attitudes and their individual outcomes—that is, a legitimization of the market as a distributor of rewards, serving as a justification for social status. Although the link between income and market justice can be tied to self-interest theories, Langsæther & Evans (2020) argues that social status does not always provide a rational explanation for attitudes toward inequality, making it necessary to test this relationship. Based on the literature, the corresponding hypothesis is:
\(H_{5}\): Individuals with higher incomes show higher education market justice preferences


3.3.3 Political ideology
Political ideology also influences people’s attitudes toward inequality. In this regard, the scientific literature has shown that people with right-wing political ideologies tend to support a market-based distribution of welfare (Lee & Stacey, 2024). Meanwhile, (Van Hootegem, 2022) found that right-wing individuals are less likely to adopt positions that support equity and equality. This finding is consistent with the study by Castillo, Iturra, et al. (2025), which found that only individuals identifying with right-wing ideologies showed a positive correlation with a preference for market justice in education. In this context, the following hypothesis is proposed:
\(H_{6}\): Right-wing individuals show higher education market justice preferences than those belonging to the left-wing


3.3.4 Moderation
Finally, I examine the moderating role of education in the relationship between meritocratic belief patterns and preferences for education market justice. Given that is expected education may play a reproductionist role, it would be interesting to observe how educational level can amplify the relationship between each latent class and education market justice preferences. Since I do not have sufficient evidence to support this hypothesis, this analysis is exploratory. Thus, the following hypothesis emerges:
\(H_{7}\): Classes that are positively associated with education market justice preferences show an amplified effect when moderated by educational level

7.2 Patterns responses
Before estimating the latent class models, we screened the eight meritocracy items (perc_effort, perc_talent, perc_rich_parents, perc_contact, pref_effort, pref_talent, pref_rich_parents, pref_contact) for careless or insufficient-effort responding (IER), following the diagnostic framework proposed by Meade & Craig (2012) and Curran (2016). We used the careless package (Yentes & Wilhelm, 2023) to compute four indicator families, each capturing a different signature of low-quality responding: (a) the longstring index, the longest run of identical consecutive responses (Johnson, 2005); (b) the intra-individual response variability (IRV), the within-person standard deviation across items (Dunn et al., 2018; Marjanovic et al., 2015); (c) the Mahalanobis distance (D²) of each response vector relative to the sample centroid, which flags multivariate outliers (Meade & Craig, 2012); and (d) the psychometric synonym/antonym scores, the within-person correlation across item pairs that are highly (positively or negatively) correlated in the overall sample (Meade & Craig, 2012). Each index was estimated separately, as they are sensitive to different response patterns (straightlining, random responding, and inconsistency, respectively) and are not expected to fully overlap.

vars_careless <- vars_m

db_careless <- db %>%
  dplyr::select(id, all_of(vars_careless)) %>%
  mutate(across(-id, as.numeric))

x_careless <- db_careless %>% dplyr::select(-id)


7.2.1 Longstring index

ls_res <- careless::longstring(x_careless, avg = TRUE)

db_careless <- db_careless %>%
  mutate(longstring = ls_res$longstr,
         avgstring  = ls_res$avgstr)

ggplot(db_careless, aes(x = longstring)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#0D0887") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(x = "Longstring index", y = "N respondents",
       caption = paste0("Source: own elaboration based on Survey EDUMERCO (n = ", nrow(db_careless), ")"))




Figura 7.3: Longstring index: longest run of identical consecutive responses (max = 8 items)








With an eight-item battery the longstring index ranges from 1 to 8. 236 respondents (6.8%) gave the same response to at least six of the eight items in a row, and 57 (1.6%) answered identically to all eight, consistent with straightlining.


7.2.2 Intra-individual response variability (IRV)

         irv_perc  = irv_res$irv1,

Because the items are ordered in two conceptual blocks (perceptions, then preferences), splitting the IRV in two (num.split = 2) yields the within-person variability separately for each block. Following Dunn et al. (2018), we flag low IRV as a marker of straightlining: 181 respondents (5.3%) fall at or below the 5th percentile of the overall IRV distribution.

We attempted the equivalent psychometric antonym score, which requires item pairs correlated at r ≤ -.60:

This is expected, since the battery contains no reverse-worded (“trap”) items by design, and it means the antonym index should be dropped from the careless-detection strategy for this study rather than forced with an unreasonably lenient threshold.


7.2.5 Combined diagnosis

  mutate(

This limited overlap is expected — longstring targets straightlining, low IRV targets low variability more generally, and Mahalanobis D² targets multivariate inconsistency — and is itself evidence against relying on any single index (Curran, 2016).
Diagnosis. Applied to the perc_/pref_ battery specifically, three conclusions follow: (1) genuine straightlining is present but concentrated in a modest subgroup (≈7% by longstring, with 57 respondents answering all eight items identically); (2) the psychometric synonym/antonym approach is only weakly informative here, because the battery is short (8 items) and deliberately heterogeneous — it crosses two response frames (perceptions vs. preferences) that the thesis treats as substantively distinct constructs, so high inter-item redundancy (needed for synonyms) and reverse-worded items (needed for antonyms) were never a design goal; consequently these two indices should be treated as secondary/diagnostic rather than as exclusion criteria; (3) longstring, IRV, and Mahalanobis D² are the most defensible indices for this instrument and should anchor any exclusion rule.
Recommendations for the latent class analysis. To “clear” careless respondents before re-estimating the LCA models in ?sec-lca-dichotomized:

Use a convergent, multi-indicator rule rather than a single cutoff: flag a respondent as likely careless only when flagged by at least two of {longstring ≥ 6, IRV ≤ p5, Mahalanobis 99% CI} (careless_2of3 above, n = 122). Single-index thresholds are somewhat arbitrary and produce more false positives.
Treat psychsyn as a secondary/reporting indicator (e.g., flag very low or negative synonym scores among respondents who already have ≥ 1 flag) rather than as a stand-alone exclusion criterion, and do not use psychant at all for this instrument.
Before dropping anyone, run a sensitivity analysis: refit the K = 1–5 poLCA models on db_lca after excluding the careless_2of3 cases, and compare AIC/BIC, entropy, class sizes, and the item-response profiles against the models already stored in output/fits_models_lca.RData. If the four-class solution and its substantive interpretation are stable, report the exclusion as a robustness check (e.g., in a footnote or appendix); if the solution changes materially, that itself is informative and should be discussed.
Prefer exclusion over imputation/weighting for the flagged cases in the main LCA, since poLCA already performs listwise deletion (na.omit()) on the dichotomized indicators; simply add dplyr::filter(!careless_2of3) (or dplyr::filter(n_flags < 2)) to the df <- db %>% select(id, ends_with("_d")) ... step used to build db_lca.
Report the number of respondents flagged and excluded (and by which criteria) in the methods section, consistent with best-practice recommendations for transparency in IER screening (Curran, 2016).

7.3 Latent class analysis with dichotomized items
We estimated latent class models with one to five classes on the sample screened for careless responding (respondents flagged by two or more of the three usable indices in Sección 7.2 were excluded beforehand). Model fit improved monotonically as the number of classes increased, as indicated by decreasing AIC and BIC values and statistically significant likelihood-ratio tests at each step (Tabla 7.3).

# ---- build table (no list-cols) -----------------------------------------

N_used <- nrow(db_lca)

m_patterns <- n_patterns_from_data(db_lca)  # scalar

# Robust extractors (avoid list-columns)

get_ll  <- function(fit) as.numeric(fit$llik)
get_aic <- function(fit) as.numeric(fit$aic)
get_bic <- function(fit) as.numeric(fit$bic)
get_npar <- function(fit) {
  if (!is.null(fit$npar)) return(as.numeric(fit$npar))
  # fallback: compute from probs
  K <- get_K(fit)
  Rj <- vapply(fit$probs, function(m) ncol(m), integer(1))
  as.numeric(sum(K * (Rj - 1)) + (K - 1))
}

# Table of fit indices

  K     = map_int(fits, get_K),
  N     = nrow(db_lca),
  logLik= map_dbl(fits, get_ll),
  npar  = map_dbl(fits, get_npar),
  AIC   = map_dbl(fits, get_aic),
  BIC   = map_dbl(fits, get_bic)
) %>%
  arrange(K) %>%
  mutate(
    # Differences relative to preceding (K-1) model
    dAIC = AIC - lag(AIC),
    dBIC = BIC - lag(BIC),
    
    # Likelihood-ratio test (K vs K-1)

    logLik = round(logLik, 1),
    npar = npar,
    AIC = round(AIC, 1),
    dAIC = round(dAIC, 1),
    BIC = round(BIC, 1),
    dBIC = round(dBIC, 1),

7.3 Four latent class model
The ?tbl-prevalence shows the conditional probabilities of each item associated with a latent class and their respective sizes. The four-class solution suggests that respondents are not primarily differentiated along a simple continuum from “more meritocratic” to “less meritocratic.” Instead, the latent classes are organized by distinct combinations of: (1) perceptions of meritocracy, (2) perceptions of non-meritocratic advantage, and (3) normative preferences regarding whether merit or privilege should determine success. As such, the results reveal heterogeneity not only in empirical diagnoses of how society works, but also in normative evaluations of whether these mechanisms are considered acceptable. This interpretation is consistent with the item-response profiles across classes.

Figura 7.6: P(endorsement | class) for each item




Class 1: Critical meritocrats (37.1%)
The first class combines low perceived meritocracy with very high perceived non-meritocracy. Respondents in this group do not believe that effort and talent are what society actually rewards, but they strongly believe that wealthy parents and social contacts shape success. Normatively, however, they strongly support meritocratic rewards and sharply reject the legitimacy of non-meritocratic advantages, especially those associated with personal networks.
This class is particularly important substantively because it captures a configuration in which meritocracy is upheld as a moral ideal while privilege is recognized as an empirical reality. In this sense, respondents in this group clearly distinguish between how society works and how it should work. They do not perceive the current system as meritocratic, but they do express strong support for a society in which effort and talent, rather than inherited or relational advantages, determine success. This class illustrates the analytical value of distinguishing perceptions from preferences, since older one-dimensional approaches to meritocratic beliefs would likely obscure this tension between normative commitment to merit and critical awareness of privilege.
Class 2: Privilege advocates (37.2%)
The second class is characterized by low perceived meritocracy and very high perceived non-meritocracy. Respondents in this group do not believe that effort or talent are strongly rewarded, but they do strongly believe that family wealth and social contacts shape life chances. At the same time, they express high support for rewarding effort and talent, yet also show high normative acceptance of advantages linked to wealthy parents and personal networks.
Substantively, this class combines a combines a realistic assessment of a stratified society with a normative justification of privilege. Thus, meritocracy is not presented as an alternative to privilege; rather, the two principles coexist and are viewed as compatible foundations for the functioning of society. This suggests a dual normative orientation in which merit and privilege are not seen as contradictory principles, but as compatible bases of social inequality.
Class 3: Universal rewards (19.0%)
The third class displays very high levels of both perceived meritocracy and perceived non-meritocracy. Respondents in this group strongly believe that effort and talent are rewarded, while also recognizing the importance of wealthy parents and social contacts. Normatively, they express very strong support for meritocratic rewards, but only moderate acceptance of non-meritocratic advantages.
This profile suggests a belief system in which merit and privilege are understood as operating simultaneously. These respondents do not deny the role of structural advantage, yet neither do they reject the view that effort and talent matter. Normatively, they strongly endorse meritocracy, while showing a more ambivalent stance toward privilege. This class can therefore be interpreted as one that sees the system as at least partially meritocratic and broadly considers this arrangement acceptable.
Class 4: Against privilege (6.7%)
The fourth class is the smallest and least clearly structured. It is characterized by a low perception of meritocracy and a low perception of the influence of privilege, specially the rich parents item. The most significant aspect of this group is that it does not perceive privilege as a factor in the distribution of resources in society, nor does it believe that it should be.

title: 5  Results
text:
7.1 Patterns responses
Before estimating the latent class models, I screened the eight meritocratic scale items for careless or insufficient-effort responding (IER), following the diagnostic framework proposed by Curran (2016). I used the careless package to compute three indicator families, each capturing a different signature of low-quality responding: (a) the longstring index, the longest run of identical consecutive responses; (b) the intra-individual response variability (IRV), the within-person standard deviation across items and (c) the Mahalanobis distance (D²) of each response vector relative to the sample centroid, which flags multivariate outliers. Each index was estimated separately, as they are sensitive to different response patterns (straightlining, random responding, and inconsistency, respectively) and are not expected to fully overlap.


Código
vars_careless <- vars_m

db_careless <- db %>%
  dplyr::select(id, all_of(vars_careless)) %>%
  mutate(across(-id, as.numeric))

x_careless <- db_careless %>% dplyr::select(-id)



7.1.1 Longstring index


Código
ls_res <- careless::longstring(x_careless, avg = TRUE)

db_careless <- db_careless %>%
  mutate(longstring = ls_res$longstr,
         avgstring  = ls_res$avgstr)

ggplot(db_careless, aes(x = longstring)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#6a1718") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(x = "Longstring index", y = "N respondents",
       caption = paste0("Source: own elaboration based on Survey EDUMERCO (n = ", nrow(db_careless), ")"))





Figura 7.1: Longstring index: longest run of identical consecutive responses (max = 8 items)








Figura 7.1 shows, as a bar chart, how many respondents reached each possible value of the index, from 1 up to 8 (the maximum, since the battery has eight items). Most respondents cluster at the low end (1 to 3 identical answers in a row): this is the expected pattern, since it means their answer changed as they moved from one item to the next, consistent with actually reading and evaluating each statement. The right side of the distribution is where straightlining shows up. It is also worth noting that, because the eight items are organized in two four-item blocks (perceptions, then preferences), a run of six or more identical responses necessarily crosses from one block into the other — so it cannot be a coincidence tied to one particular question, but reflects the same answer being carried across two conceptually different sets of items. With an eight-item battery the longstring index ranges from 1 to 8. 236 respondents (6.8%) gave the same response to at least six of the eight items in a row, and 57 (1.6%) answered identically to all eight, consistent with straightlining.


7.1.2 Intra-individual response variability (IRV)


Código
irv_res <- careless::irv(x_careless, na.rm = TRUE, split = TRUE, num.split = 2)

db_careless <- db_careless %>%
  mutate(irv_total = irv_res$irvTotal,
         irv_perc  = irv_res$irv1,
         irv_pref  = irv_res$irv2)

db_careless %>%
  dplyr::select(id, `Overall (8 items)` = irv_total,
                `Perceptions block` = irv_perc,
                `Preferences block` = irv_pref) %>%
  pivot_longer(-id, names_to = "block", values_to = "irv") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = irv)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#6a1718") +
  facet_wrap(~block, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "IRV", y = "N respondents")





Figura 7.2: Intra-individual response variability (IRV), overall and by item block








The IRV summarizes, for each respondent, how much their own answers moved across the eight items: someone who marks the same option (or nearly so) throughout the battery gets a low IRV, while someone who uses different points of the scale gets a higher one. In the histograms above, respondents piling up near zero (left side) are those whose answers were essentially flat — the pattern expected from careless or straightlined responding — while respondents further to the right made more use of the response scale, as most people do. Because the items are ordered in two conceptual blocks (perceptions, then preferences), splitting the IRV in two (num.split = 2) shows this same left-to-right pattern separately for each block, which also reveals whether flat responding is concentrated in only one part of the questionnaire rather than spread across the whole battery. Following Dunn et al. (2018), we flag low IRV as a marker of straightlining: 181 respondents (5.3%) fall at or below the 5th percentile of the overall IRV distribution — i.e., the flattest 5% of the sample.


7.1.3 Mahalanobis distance


Código
mahad_res <- careless::mahad(x_careless, plot = FALSE, flag = TRUE, confidence = 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)

db_careless <- db_careless %>%
  mutate(mahad_d = mahad_res$d_sq,
         mahad_flag = mahad_res$flagged)

ggplot(db_careless, aes(x = mahad_d, fill = mahad_flag)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "grey70", "TRUE" = "#6a1718"), name = "Flagged (99% CI)") +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Mahalanobis ", D^2)), y = "N respondents")





Figura 7.3: Mahalanobis D² of item-response vectors, flagged at the 99% confidence level








The Mahalanobis distance takes a different approach from the previous two indices: instead of looking at a respondent’s answers on their own, it compares each respondent’s whole pattern of answers against the pattern that is typical for the sample as a whole — taking into account how the eight items normally relate to one another (e.g., that seeing wealthy parents as an advantage tends to go together with seeing personal contacts as one). A person can therefore give variable, non-repetitive answers and still get a high Mahalanobis distance if the combination of their answers is unusual given how the items normally move together in the rest of the sample; this is why the index is described as multivariate rather than item-by-item. In the histogram, respondents piled up on the left have D² values close to zero, meaning their overall response pattern is unremarkable, while the tail stretching to the right holds respondents whose combined pattern departs the most from what is typical. Bars are colored to mark which of these are flagged as outliers under a 99% confidence threshold (grey = within the expected range, red = flagged) — a deliberately conservative cutoff, so only the most extreme patterns are marked. At this conservative 99% confidence level, 205 respondents (6%) are flagged as multivariate outliers relative to the response distribution of the other eight items.


7.1.4 Combined diagnosis


Código
careless_flags <- db_careless %>%
  mutate(
    flag_longstring = longstring >= 6,
    flag_irv        = irv_total <= quantile(irv_total, .05, na.rm = TRUE),
    flag_mahad      = mahad_flag,
    n_flags         = rowSums(across(c(flag_longstring, flag_irv, flag_mahad)), na.rm = TRUE),
    careless_2of3   = n_flags >= 2
  )

careless_flags %>%
  count(n_flags) %>%
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  kableExtra::kable(format = "html", align = "c",

                    caption = NULL) %>%

                            bootstrap_options = c("striped", "bordered", "condensed"))

To check whether the four-class solution is an artifact of dichotomizing the items, I re-estimated the latent class models on the eight original 4-category items, keeping the full ordinal response scale instead of collapsing it to a binary indicator. Figura 7.9: Mean expected item score (1-4) by class, ordinal items




The four-class solution estimated on the ordinal items has a markedly different class structure from the dichotomized solution: 27.4%, 17.8%, 19.9%, and 34.9% of respondents, respectively — compared with 6.7%, 19.0%, 37.2%, and 37.1% in the dichotomized model. Substantively:

Class 1 (27.4%): Shows moderate-to-low agreement on perceived merit and, distinctively, only moderate agreement that privilege factors matter. This is the largest class under the ordinal model.
Class 2 (17.8%): Shows the highest agreement on perceived merit combined with high perceived privilege and strong preference for merit-based rewards, but only moderate acceptance of privilege advantage — resembling the dichotomized “Universal rewards” class.
Class 3 (19.9%): Combines low perceived merit with very high perceived privilege, strong preference for merit-based rewards, and low acceptance of privilege advantage — resembling the dichotomized “Critical meritocrats” class, though notably smaller here.
Class 4 (34.9%): Also combines low perceived merit with very high perceived privilege and strong preference for merit-based rewards, but shows only moderate (rather than high or low) acceptance of privilege advantage.

title: 5  Results
text:
5.3 Preliminary conclusions
Based on the analysis for this installment, there are three points worth mentioning in conclusion
1) After analyzing careless respondents and eliminating those cases, the fundamental structure of the latent classes remained intact, with only slight variations in their sizes. This means that the classes identified are robust in the face of careless responses and, therefore, are accurate representations of people’s beliefs.
2) When latent class analysis was applied without dichotomizing the variables, the fit indices were less clear in the optimal class solution. Specifically, the 4- to 5-class solution did not allow us to conclude that the 4-class model was the most balanced. This might suggest that, by not dichotomizing the variables, there could be other variations in the class solution that would be worth exploring in the future.
3) In the analysis of latent classes without dichotomization, no equivalence was found with the previously observed classes (dichotomized LCA), but there are similarities worth noting. While Class 1 does not have a very clear equivalent, Class 2 can be associated with Universal Rewards due to the similarity in their profiles. On the other hand, Classes 3 and 4 share a fairly similar structure, except that Class 3 is more opposed to the idea that privilege factors operate in society. In this sense, these classes largely share the characteristics of Critical Meritocrats.

Figura 4.1: Market justice in education (diverging Likert plot)





Figura 4.1 shows the distribution of responses on market justice in education. Rejection clearly predominates: 78% of respondents disagree with the statement (38% strongly disagree and 40% disagree), whereas only 22% agree (16% agree and 6% strongly agree). Responses are evenly split between the two disagreement categories, while strong agreement is marginal. Although this suggests that the idea that access to better education should depend on the ability to pay has little legitimacy, we must not overlook the fact that more than one-fifth of the sample supports the commodification of education, which could have significant consequences for the legitimization of educational inequality.

Figura 4.2: Polychoric correlations between meritocracy indicators and market justice in education (* p < .05, ** p < .01, *** p < .001)





Figura 4.2 shows the polychoric correlations between the meritocracy indicators and market justice in education. Regarding market justice in education, the strongest associations are with the preference for parental wealth (r = .33) and for contacts (r = .33), indicating that those who consider these privilege factors legitimate are more likely to justify a market-based education. The perception that parental wealth (r = −.19) and contacts (r = −.21) matter in Chile shows a weaker association with market justice in education in the opposite direction. The correlations with merit indicators are small (|r| ≤ .17). Among the indicators, the strongest correlations are those within each dimension: effort and talent (perceived r = .70; preferred r = .47), and parental wealth and contacts (perceived r = .74; preferred r = .72), which supports the distinction between merit and privilege dimensions. Across the results, the only moderate correlations are between perceived non-merit factors and preferred effort (.38 for parental wealth and .43 for contacts).

Figura 4.3 presents the standardized estimates of the structural equation model, which includes age, education, sex, income quintiles and political orientation as control variables (omitted from the figure for clarity). The model fits the data well (scaled CFI = .959, TLI = .985, RMSEA = .046, 90% CI [.043, .049], SRMR = .037). Also, the measurement model is satisfactory: all standardized loadings are significant and range from .55 to .92, with the privilege factors being particularly well defined (.81 to .90). Regarding the structural paths, preferences for privilege factor show the strongest association with market justice in education (\(\beta\) = .32, p < .001), indicating that individuals who favor non-meritocratic criteria are more likely to justify a market-based education system. In contrast, perceptions of privilege factors are negatively associated with market justice (\(\beta\) = −.20, p < .001): those who perceive that parental wealth and contacts shape opportunities in Chile are less likely to endorse a market-based education. Perceived merit has a very small positive effect (\(\beta\) = .05, p < .05), while preferred merit is not significantly related to the outcome (\(\beta\) = .04, p = .294). Overall, market justice in education is shaped mainly by beliefs about privilege criteria rather than by meritocratic ones, and perceptions and preferences operate in opposite directions in meritocratic dimension.


4.1.3 Latent class analysis
We estimated latent class models with one to five classes. Model fit improved monotonically as the number of classes increased, as indicated by decreasing AIC and BIC values and statistically significant likelihood-ratio tests at each step (Tabla 4.1).


Código
# ---- build table (no list-cols) -----------------------------------------

N_used <- nrow(db_lca)

m_patterns <- n_patterns_from_data(db_lca)  # scalar

# Robust extractors (avoid list-columns)
get_K <- function(fit) as.integer(ncol(fit$posterior))  # classes = cols of posterior
get_ll  <- function(fit) as.numeric(fit$llik)
get_aic <- function(fit) as.numeric(fit$aic)
get_bic <- function(fit) as.numeric(fit$bic)
get_npar <- function(fit) {
  if (!is.null(fit$npar)) return(as.numeric(fit$npar))
  # fallback: compute from probs
  K <- get_K(fit)
  Rj <- vapply(fit$probs, function(m) ncol(m), integer(1))
  as.numeric(sum(K * (Rj - 1)) + (K - 1))
}

# Table of fit indices
fit_tbl <- tibble(
  K     = map_int(fits, get_K),
  N     = nrow(db_lca),
  logLik= map_dbl(fits, get_ll),
  npar  = map_dbl(fits, get_npar),
  AIC   = map_dbl(fits, get_aic),
  BIC   = map_dbl(fits, get_bic)
) %>%
  arrange(K) %>%
  mutate(
    # Differences relative to preceding (K-1) model
    dAIC = AIC - lag(AIC),
    dBIC = BIC - lag(BIC),
    
    # Likelihood-ratio test (K vs K-1)
    # Test statistic: 2*(LL_K - LL_{K-1}) ~ Chi-square with df = npar_K - npar_{K-1}
    # Note: in LCA, models are not strictly nested in the regular sense;
    # this LRT is widely used as a heuristic, but interpret with caution.
    LRT = 2 * (logLik - lag(logLik)),
    df_LRT = npar - lag(npar),
    p_LRT = ifelse(!is.na(LRT) & df_LRT > 0, pchisq(LRT, df = df_LRT, lower.tail = FALSE), NA_real_)
  )


fit_tbl_report <- fit_tbl %>%
  transmute(
    K, N,
    logLik = round(logLik, 1),
    npar = npar,
    AIC = round(AIC, 1),
    dAIC = round(dAIC, 1),
    BIC = round(BIC, 1),
    dBIC = round(dBIC, 1),
    LRT = round(LRT, 1),
    df_LRT = df_LRT,

Class 1: Critical meritocrats (37.1%)
The first class combines low perceived meritocracy with very high perceived non-meritocracy. Respondents in this group do not believe that effort and talent are what society actually rewards, but they strongly believe that wealthy parents and social contacts shape success. Normatively, however, they strongly support meritocratic rewards and sharply reject the legitimacy of non-meritocratic advantages, especially those associated with personal networks.
This class is particularly important substantively because it captures a configuration in which meritocracy is upheld as a moral ideal while privilege is recognized as an empirical reality. In this sense, respondents in this group clearly distinguish between how society works and how it should work. They do not perceive the current system as meritocratic, but they do express strong support for a society in which effort and talent, rather than inherited or relational advantages, determine success. This class illustrates the analytical value of distinguishing perceptions from preferences, since older one-dimensional approaches to meritocratic beliefs would likely obscure this tension between normative commitment to merit and critical awareness of privilege.
Class 2: Privilege advocates (37.2%)
The second class is characterized by low perceived meritocracy and very high perceived non-meritocracy. Respondents in this group do not believe that effort or talent are strongly rewarded, but they do strongly believe that family wealth and social contacts shape life chances. At the same time, they express high support for rewarding effort and talent, yet also show high normative acceptance of advantages linked to wealthy parents and personal networks.
Substantively, this class combines a combines a realistic assessment of a stratified society with a normative justification of privilege. Thus, meritocracy is not presented as an alternative to privilege; rather, the two principles coexist and are viewed as compatible foundations for the functioning of society. This suggests a dual normative orientation in which merit and privilege are not seen as contradictory principles, but as compatible bases of social inequality.
Class 3: Universal rewards (19.0%)
The third class displays very high levels of both perceived meritocracy and perceived non-meritocracy. Respondents in this group strongly believe that effort and talent are rewarded, while also recognizing the importance of wealthy parents and social contacts. Normatively, they express very strong support for meritocratic rewards, but only moderate acceptance of non-meritocratic advantages.
This profile suggests a belief system in which merit and privilege are understood as operating simultaneously. These respondents do not deny the role of structural advantage, yet neither do they reject the view that effort and talent matter. Normatively, they strongly endorse meritocracy, while showing a more ambivalent stance toward privilege. This class can therefore be interpreted as one that sees the system as at least partially meritocratic and broadly considers this arrangement acceptable.
Class 4: Against privilege (6.7%)
The fourth class is the smallest and least clearly structured. It is characterized by a low perception of meritocracy and a low perception of the influence of privilege, specially the rich parents item. The most significant aspect of this group is that it does not perceive privilege as a factor in the distribution of resources in society, nor does it believe that it should be.

Tabla 4.2 reports four ordinal logistic regressions of market justice in education. Model 1 includes only latent class membership, Model 2 only the sociodemographic and political variables (sex, university education, income quintile and political identification), Model 3 both sets of predictors, Model 4 adds the interaction between latent class and university education to the full model, Model 5 the interaction between latent class and sex, and Model 6 the interaction between latent class and political identification. In Model 1, members of the other three classes have significantly higher odds of endorsing market justice in education than the Critical meritocrats (reference): Privilege advocates (OR = 2.50, 95% CI [2.10, 2.97]), Universal rewards (OR = 2.32, [1.88, 2.86]) and Against privilege (OR = 2.55, [1.85, 3.53]). The three coefficients are similar and their confidence intervals overlap, so the main contrast is between the Critical meritocrats and the remaining classes rather than among the latter. Model 2 shows that women (OR = 0.66) and people with university education (OR = 0.84) have lower odds of market justice, while those identifying with the center (OR = 2.03), the right (OR = 2.98) or not identifying with any position (OR = 1.75) have higher odds than those on the left; income quintiles are not significantly associated with the outcome. In the full model (Model 3), the class coefficients decrease moderately (ORs between 2.04 and 2.28) but remain significant, and the coefficients of the remaining variables change little, with the exception of political identification, whose odds ratios for the center and the right fall from 2.03 to 1.78 and from 2.98 to 2.63. This indicates that the association between latent classes and market justice is not explained by sociodemographic characteristics, although part of it overlaps with political orientation, and that the classes capture belief configurations that are related to, but distinct from, ideological position. Model 3 also has the best fit (AIC = 5,687.9 versus 5,798.0 and 5,777.0 for Models 1 and 2; BIC = 5,775.2 versus 5,832.9 and 5,846.8), so both sets of predictors contribute independently to explaining market justice in education. Finally, Model 4 shows no evidence that the association between latent classes and market justice varies by educational level: none of the interactions between class membership and university education were statistically significant (Privilege advocates OR = 1.03, [0.72, 1.48]; Universal rewards OR = 0.94, [0.61, 1.44]; Against privilege OR = 0.94, [0.47, 1.89]), and the model fits worse than Model 3 (AIC = 5,693.7; BIC = 5,798.4). Models 5 and 6 lead to the same conclusion for sex and political identification. In Model 5 none of the class-by-sex interactions is significant (Privilege advocates OR = 0.91, [0.64, 1.28]; Universal rewards OR = 0.86, [0.56, 1.31]; Against privilege OR = 0.70, [0.36, 1.35]), and in Model 6 none of the nine class-by-political-identification interactions reaches conventional significance either, the closest being Against privilege x Right (OR = 0.39, [0.15, 1.06]). Likelihood-ratio tests against Model 3 confirm that neither set of interactions improves the fit (sex: \(\chi^2\)(3) = 1.34, p = .721; political identification: \(\chi^2\)(9) = 13.37, p = .147), and both models have higher BIC than Model 3 (5,797.3 and 5,832.2 versus 5,775.2). The association between latent classes and market justice in education is therefore similar across sex, educational level and political orientation.
