title: 3  Theoretical and empirical background
text:
3.2 Meritocratic and privilege beliefs
When discussing education, it is difficult not to encounter the concept of meritocracy. Based on Michael Young’s work The Rise of Meritocracy (1962) (2017), this concept is understood as the distribution of rewards based on effort and talent. In the school context, credentials function as awards that reflect students’ performance in various subjects. In this sense, meritocracy is a fundamental element of every educational institution, as it is one of the principles governing the awarding of credentials. Beyond that, meritocratic ideals are promoted in a narrative that merit can reflect in a inmediate way and is socially meaningful as can provide rewards and social mobility (Batruch et al., 2023; Traini, 2022). Thus, beliefs about the educational system are often closely tied to meritocracy (Clycq et al., 2014; Darnon et al., 2018).
In the field of education, meritocracy has been used as a distributive principle, but within this framework, it has also been linked to the justification of inequalities. Starting from Adams’ theory of equity (1963), meritocracy operates as a universal equality principle, where rewards should be commensurate with effort. Several studies have shown that meritocratic beliefs are associated with individualistic beliefs, such as an aversion to redistribution and a preference for market justice (Bartram, 2023; Castillo et al., 2024; Castillo, Iturra, et al., 2025; Mijs, 2021; Sin et al., 2026), and are characteristic of those in more privileged social positions (Heuer et al., 2020). In these cases, meritocracy is used to legitimize positions, with those who benefit from the system often justifying their success on the basis of their own merit, overlooking the structural conditions that shape reality. Thus, the merit narrative is linked to support the idea that money should determine the quality and access to education. This normative judgment runs counter to educational justice, as it hinders equal opportunities and, ultimately, determines students’ educational trajectories (Moyano, 2020; Walzer, 2010).
In the meritocracy research framework, most studies have used surveys to respond their research questions, with the ISSP as the main instrument for measuring and analyzing meritocratic beliefs in both national and international contexts. These items show the relevance of meritocratic factors for getting ahead in life, like effort and talent, and also consider inherited conditions as contacts, for instance. Following this conceptual model, there is a tradition of studying meritocratic beliefs from a unidimensional perspective (García-Sánchez et al., 2019; Mijs, 2021). The problem with this approach is that it has serious implications for understanding social reality, since it assumes that people’s beliefs follow a rational logic in which, if a belief in meritocracy is stronger, a belief in privilege must be weaker. To address this, in recent years, some authors have proposed a multidimensional perspective on meritocracy, constructing frameworks that allow for distinguishing the dimension of merit from that of privilege, on the one hand, and differentiating perceptions from preferences on the other (Castillo et al., 2023; Zhu, 2025).
Previous research using a multidimensional approach to merit and privilege has revealed that meritocratic beliefs and those based on privilege can coexist in people’s minds, suggesting that individuals may simultaneously hold beliefs that appear contradictory (Castillo et al., 2023). Within this framework, some studies have highlighted the importance of meritocracy and privilege, as people may exhibit a disconnect between what they say and what they actually prefer. Khan & Jerolmack (2013) demonstrate that elite students rely on merit as a discursive and identity-forming resource, but that does not mean they reject privilege. As Grompone & Reategui (2025) argues, schools play a fundamental role in the production of privilege, so it is essential to examine this concept alongside merit when discussing inequalities in education. Nevertheless, there are a caveat regarding the individuals who hold these beliefs. We do not know how these beliefs are distributed across the population. In other words, although we know that meritocratic and privilege beliefs can coexist, we do not know how the various combinations of these dimensions interact in people’s minds, how prevalent they are in the population, or how they relate to market justice in education. To address this issue, I propose a Latent Profile Analysis (LPA), a person-centered approach that allows us to identify the heterogeneity of beliefs by clustering individuals, offering insights that differ from variable-centered methods, which assume that the association between two or more variables in the population behaves uniformly (Cech & Blair-Loy, 2010).
Although LPA allows us to identify different configurations of meritocratic beliefs, it is not possible to define in advance the exact types of patterns that will be found. In this regard, the evidence suggests that one of the most likely patterns is a predominant meritocratic beliefs, in which individuals consider merit important and structural factors unimportant (Heuer et al., 2020; Xian & Reynolds, 2017; Zhu, 2025). On the other hand, a pattern has also been identified in which success is attributed to family and background conditions rather than effort (C. Palomino & Sebastian, 2026). Finally, a pattern of dual consciousness has been identified, in which individuals consider merit, family connections, and wealth to be important (Zhu, 2025). Therefore, based on previous studies, this research expect to find at least three types of groups based on meritocratic beliefs: a meritocratic-dominant profile; a profile characterized by aware of privilege, and finally a dual consciousness class, viewing merits and privilege factors as important simultaneously.
Each pattern of meritocratic beliefs can be situated within a framework of meaning related to a preference for market justice in education. As the literature suggests, the perception of meritocracy is widely associated with the legitimization of inequalities—and specifically with market justice—so it is to be expected that the first group would adhere to this pattern (Castillo, Laffert, et al., 2025; Castillo, Iturra, et al., 2025). With regard to the second group, the prevalence of privilege could be directly associated with disagreement over education-market justice preferences, since observing that society distributes rewards based on factors unrelated to merit might seem unfair (Alesina & La Ferrara, 2005). Finally, the pattern of dual consciousness may demonstrate that the recognition of merit and privilege in the functioning of society could imply an understanding that structural conditions play an important role in individual outcomes, leading to opposition to the idea that access to and the quality of a service such as education should be based on economic conditions (Xian & Reynolds, 2017; Zhu, 2025).

title: 3  Theoretical and empirical background
text:
3.3 Status, political ideology and moderation

3.3.1 Education
There are various theories regarding how educational attainment affects people’s redistributive preferences. On the one hand, there are theories that view education as a resource that enhances the development of technical skills and/or critical thinking, leading individuals to become aware of structural problems and, as a result, to support the reduction of inequality (Becker, 1993; Freire, 2015; Schultz, 1961). On the other hand, in cultural reproduction theories, education has been understood as a source of social inequalities, as it reproduces individuals’ living conditions, preventing opportunities for intergenerational social mobility and, consequently, perpetuating the stratified social order (Bourdieu, 2019; Bowles & Gintis, 2011). Within the framework of redistributive preferences, reproductionist notions are grounded in self-interest theory, whereby those with higher levels of education tend to exhibit attitudes that reflect a desire to protect their privileged social positions, which could be understood as an aversion to redistribution or support for market-based justice. Thus, education can be understood not only as an enlightening force in social life but also as a cog in the reproduction of inequalities.
Recent literature provides empirical support for both reproductionist and enlightenment approaches to education. In support of the reproductionist approach, research by Nye et al. (2026) found, in an analysis of 282 country-year combinations from various international surveys, that in 95% of cases, individual educational level was positively associated with market-oriented attitudes. Likewise, Van Noord et al. (2019) used data from 31 countries to show that education is widely understood as the basis for social stratification. In support of the enlightenment approach, Busemeyer (2012) found that higher levels of education are associated with a greater preference for public investment. However, the results from Liu & Wang (2026) suggest that education does not fulfill a generalized function; rather, both the enlightening and the reproductionist roles coexist but depend on the level of education. In countries with low inequality, basic education is associated with reproductionist positions, while secondary and tertiary education highlight the enlightening role.


3.3.2 Income
In addition to educational level, the literature has shown that income is also an important factor in the study of attitudes toward inequality (Heuer et al., 2020; Lindh, 2015). The evidence shows that higher-income individuals tend to support market-based distributive principles (Immergut & Schneider, 2020; Lindh, 2015; Nye et al., 2026). In this context, among higher-status social groups, there is congruence between their attitudes and their individual outcomes—that is, a legitimization of the market as a distributor of rewards, serving as a justification for social status. Although the link between income and market justice can be tied to self-interest theories, Langsæther & Evans (2020) argues that social status does not always provide a rational explanation for attitudes toward inequality, making it necessary to test this relationship.


3.3.3 Political ideology
Political ideology also influences people’s attitudes toward inequality. In this regard, the scientific literature has shown that people with right-wing political ideologies tend to support a market-based distribution of welfare (Lee & Stacey, 2024). Meanwhile, (Van Hootegem, 2022) found that right-wing individuals are less likely to adopt positions that support equity and equality. This finding is consistent with the study by Castillo, Iturra, et al. (2025), which found that only individuals identifying with right-wing ideologies showed a positive correlation with a preference for market justice in education.


3.3.4 Moderation
Finally, I examine the moderating role of education in the relationship between meritocratic belief patterns and preferences for education market justice. Given that is expected education may play a reproductionist role, it would be interesting to observe how educational level can amplify the relationship between each latent class and education market justice preferences. Since I do not have sufficient evidence to support this hypothesis, this analysis is exploratory.

title: 5  Results
text:
5.1 Descriptives
This section is structured as follows: First, we present the descriptive results to provide an overview of how beliefs regarding market justice, as well as those regarding merit and privilege, are distributed. Second, we present the LPA, explaining how the final solution was reached and illustrating the characteristics of the individuals who make up each profile. Finally, the relationship between each of the latent profiles and market justice in education is analyzed, including the other independent variables.
Figure 5.1: Market justice in education (diverging Likert plot)
Figure 5.1 shows the distribution of responses on market justice in education. Rejection clearly predominates: 78% of respondents disagree with the statement (38% strongly disagree and 40% disagree), whereas only 22% agree (16% agree and 6% strongly agree). Responses are evenly split between the two disagreement categories, while strong agreement is marginal. Although this suggests that the idea that access to better education should depend on the ability to pay has little legitimacy, we must not overlook the fact that more than one-fifth of the sample supports the commodification of education, which could have significant consequences for the legitimization of educational inequality.
Figure 5.2: Perceptions and preferences about success factors (Likert plot)
Figure 5.2 contrasts perceptions (panel A) with preferences (panel B) about success factors, and the gap between the two is the most salient result. Perceptions are dominated by non-meritocratic factors: 94% agree that contacts and 87% that rich parents matter for getting ahead in Chile (59% and 54% strongly agree), whereas only 28% perceive that effort and 38% that talent are rewarded. Preferences show an almost mirrored pattern: 92% think effort should matter (56% strongly agree) and 73% talent, while support for rich parents (50%) and contacts (45%) falls sharply and is split almost evenly between agreement and disagreement. The gaps are therefore large and run in opposite directions: for effort, agreement rises by 64 percentage points from perceptions to preferences (28% to 92%) and for talent by 35 points (38% to 73%), while for rich parents it falls by 37 points (87% to 50%) and for contacts by 49 points (94% to 45%). In average terms (1–4 scale), preferences exceed perceptions by 1.33 points for effort and 0.73 for talent, and fall below them by 0.95 for rich parents and 1.14 for contacts (all paired Wilcoxon tests, p < .001). Overall, respondents describe an unmeritocratic society (success is perceived to depend on origin and connections) and express a clear preference for a meritocratic one, with effort as the most valued factor. Notably, a non-trivial share still endorses rich parents and contacts as legitimate determinants of success.
Figure 5.3: Polychoric correlations between meritocracy indicators and market justice in education (* p < .05, ** p < .01, *** p < .001)
Figure 5.3 shows the polychoric correlations between the meritocracy indicators and market justice in education. Regarding market justice in education, the strongest associations are with the preference for parental wealth (r = .33) and for contacts (r = .33), indicating that those who consider these privilege factors legitimate are more likely to justify a market-based education. In contrast, the perception that parental wealth (r = −.19) and contacts (r = −.21) matter in Chile shows a weaker association with market justice in education in the opposite direction. The correlations with merit indicators are small (|r| ≤ .17). Among the indicators, the strongest correlations are those within each dimension: effort and talent (perceived r = .70; preferred r = .47), and parental wealth and contacts (perceived r = .74; preferred r = .72), which supports the distinction between merit and privilege dimensions. Across the results, the only moderate correlations are between perceived non-merit factors and preferred effort (.38 for parental wealth and .43 for contacts).

The gaps are therefore large and run in opposite directions: for effort, agreement rises by 64 percentage points from perceptions to preferences (28% to 92%) and for talent by 35 points (38% to 73%), while for rich parents it falls by 37 points (87% to 50%) and for contacts by 49 points (94% to 45%). In average terms (1–4 scale), preferences exceed perceptions by 1.33 points for effort and 0.73 for talent, and fall below them by 0.95 for rich parents and 1.14 for contacts (all paired Wilcoxon tests, p < .001). Overall, respondents describe an unmeritocratic society (success is perceived to depend on origin and connections) and express a clear preference for a meritocratic one, with effort as the most valued factor. Notably, a non-trivial share still endorses rich parents and contacts as legitimate determinants of success.

Figura 4.3 shows the polychoric correlations between the meritocracy indicators and market justice in education. Regarding market justice in education, the strongest associations are with the preference for parental wealth (r = .33) and for contacts (r = .33), indicating that those who consider these privilege factors legitimate are more likely to justify a market-based education. In contrast, the perception that parental wealth (r = −.19) and contacts (r = −.21) matter in Chile shows a weaker association with market justice in education in the opposite direction. The correlations with merit indicators are small (|r| ≤ .17). Among the indicators, the strongest correlations are those within each dimension: effort and talent (perceived r = .70; preferred r = .47), and parental wealth and contacts (perceived r = .74; preferred r = .72), which supports the distinction between merit and privilege dimensions. Across the results, the only moderate correlations are between perceived non-merit factors and preferred effort (.38 for parental wealth and .43 for contacts).

title: 3  Theoretical and empirical background
text:
3.3 Status and political ideology

3.3.1 Education
There are various theories regarding how educational attainment affects people’s redistributive preferences. On the one hand, there are theories that view education as a resource that enhances the development of technical skills and/or critical thinking, leading individuals to become aware of structural problems and, as a result, to support the reduction of inequality (Becker, 1993; Freire, 2015; Schultz, 1961). On the other hand, in cultural reproduction theories, education has been understood as a source of social inequalities, as it reproduces individuals’ living conditions, preventing opportunities for intergenerational social mobility and, consequently, perpetuating the stratified social order (Bourdieu, 2019; Bowles & Gintis, 2011). Within the framework of redistributive preferences, reproductionist notions are grounded in self-interest theory, whereby those with higher levels of education tend to exhibit attitudes that reflect a desire to protect their privileged social positions, which could be understood as an aversion to redistribution or support for market-based justice. Thus, education can be understood not only as an enlightening force in social life but also as a cog in the reproduction of inequalities.
Recent literature provides empirical support for both reproductionist and enlightenment approaches to education. In support of the reproductionist approach, research by Nye et al. (2026) found, in an analysis of 282 country-year combinations from various international surveys, that in 95% of cases, individual educational level was positively associated with market-oriented attitudes. Likewise, Van Noord et al. (2019) used data from 31 countries to show that education is widely understood as the basis for social stratification. In support of the enlightenment approach, Busemeyer (2012) found that higher levels of education are associated with a greater preference for public investment. However, the results from Liu & Wang (2026) suggest that education does not fulfill a generalized function; rather, both the enlightening and the reproductionist roles coexist but depend on the level of education. In countries with low inequality, basic education is associated with reproductionist positions, while secondary and tertiary education highlight the enlightening role.


3.3.2 Income
In addition to educational level, the literature has shown that income is also an important factor in the study of attitudes toward inequality (Heuer et al., 2020; Lindh, 2015). The evidence shows that higher-income individuals tend to support market-based distributive principles (Immergut & Schneider, 2020; Lindh, 2015; Nye et al., 2026). In this context, among higher-status social groups, there is congruence between their attitudes and their individual outcomes—that is, a legitimization of the market as a distributor of rewards, serving as a justification for social status. Although the link between income and market justice can be tied to self-interest theories, Langsæther & Evans (2020) argues that social status does not always provide a rational explanation for attitudes toward inequality, making it necessary to test this relationship.


3.3.3 Political ideology
Political ideology also influences people’s attitudes toward inequality. In this regard, the scientific literature has shown that people with right-wing political ideologies tend to support a market-based distribution of welfare (Lee & Stacey, 2024). Meanwhile, (Van Hootegem, 2022) found that right-wing individuals are less likely to adopt positions that support equity and equality. This finding is consistent with the study by Castillo, Iturra, et al. (2025), which found that only individuals identifying with right-wing ideologies showed a positive association with a preference for market justice in education.
Based on international and national evidence regarding the identity-driven shift occurring across the political spectrum, particularly on the right (Alenda, 2023; Häusermann et al., 2026), this study aims to examine the interaction between latent profiles and political identification to determine whether identification with a particular political sector intensifies or attenuates the relationship between latent profiles and market justice in education. Since I lack information to support any specific hypothesis, this analysis is exploratory.

title: 6  Discussion
text:
Previous research has found a positive relationship between meritocratic beliefs and market justice in education. However, the purpose of this study is, first and foremost, to demonstrate that meritocratic beliefs must be examined alongside beliefs about privilege, addressing both individual and structural explanations that may account for success. More specifically, the main objective is to demonstrate that there are groups with different configurations of meritocratic and privilege beliefs, which have divergent relationships with market justice in education. Therefore, a person-centered method was applied to construct typologies based on merit and privilege, and then to study their relationship with market justice in education.
The study’s results identified three latent profiles that combined perceptions and preferences regarding merit and privilege: a profile that combined strong preferences for meritocracy and weak preferences for privilege; a profile that showed similar preferences for both meritocratic and privilege factors; and, finally, a profile that perceived privilege to a lesser extent than the previous two, combined with moderate preferences for both meritocracy and privilege. The first two profiles described can be partially aligned with those found by Zhu (2025), supporting one latent group characterized by a prevailing adherence to meritocracy and another with dual awareness, which recognizes the role of both individual and structural conditions. However, the findings of this research show that these profiles differ fundamentally in their preferences regarding privilege; while the meritocratic profile rejects them, the other embraces them. This reflects that support for or rejection of privilege is a fundamental characteristic for elucidating various patterns of belief. On the other hand, the third profile cannot be linked to the same background factors. One possible interpretation for this group is that these are individuals with a naive attitude toward how society functions (as they have the lowest perception of privilege), in addition to maintaining a passive attitude toward social reality, where moderate preferences seem to be an idea internalized by the system rather than a value that drives these individuals’ normative judgments.
By focusing on the relationship between latent profiles and market justice in education, we find something new: the configurations of meritocratic beliefs and privilege embodied by the profiles determine the legitimization of educational inequalities in different ways. Figure 5.8 already suggests a distinct relationship between the “Congruent Meritocrats” and the other two profiles, while the regression model reconfirms this. This finding is key, as it challenges the positive relationship between meritocracy and market preferences—a relationship supported in the literature by hypotheses of self-interest or the adoption of the meritocratic narrative as a justification for social status (Bartram, 2023; Castillo et al., 2024; Castillo, Laffert, et al., 2025; Castillo et al., 2026; Heuer et al., 2020). Here, the existence of “Congruent Meritocrats” demonstrates that a strong belief in meritocracy does not necessarily lead to a greater preference for market-based criteria. In this case, the pattern of beliefs that defines the profile helps explain the reason for this relationship: because they perceive that privilege is rewarded in society at the expense of merit, they prefer merit as the primary factor in the distribution of rewards. This aversion to privilege is ultimately consistent with opposing the idea that the ability to pay should be a determining factor in accessing a good education. The other two profiles offer a different explanation: the coexistence of merit and privilege in its ascriptive dimension leads to support for the idea that basic socioeconomic conditions should determine the education people receive. Thus, this dual perspective held by privilege advocates does not imply a challenge to structural conditions, but rather acknowledges—and even endorses—that privileges should function as a distributive criterion at the societal and educational levels. This may be related to studies such as those by Khan & Jerolmack (2013) and Gogescu (2024), which suggest that the recognition of merit coexists with the protection of privileges. Another explanation can be found in the ideas put forward by Scharff (2021), who notes that in a context of high inequality such as Chile’s, some people view this reality as inevitable and would therefore prefer to use any resource at their disposal to advance their careers. Thus, by examining meritocracy alongside privilege, we can highlight that the meritocratic narrative can legitimize inequalities, but it can also serve as a mechanism to mitigate educational disparities.
Education was found to have an effect opposite to that posited in \(H_{1}\); therefore, there is no evidence in support of this hypothesis. The data indicate that a higher level of education is negatively associated with market justice in education, demonstrating that educational training fosters a perspective capable of recognizing the role that structural conditions play in the access to and quality of social services—such as education—and opposes this (Busemeyer, 2012; Freire, 2015). This perspective is associated with what the literature has termed the “enlightening effect” of education. While this finding runs counter to the posits of authors such as Nye et al. (2026) or Van Noord et al. (2019), it is important to consider the regional and national context. In a region such as Latin America—historically marked by conflicts that repeatedly bring inequality and the influence of socioeconomic conditions on life trajectories to the forefront—education may have a more decisive illuminating effect than in regions with greater well-being (Dussel, 2019). In contrast, income did not show a significant effect in any of its quintiles; therefore, there is insufficient evidence to support \(H_{2}\). Furthermore, a Bottom/Middle/Top operationalization (40/50/10) was tested, but no effects were found there either.
The relationship between political identification and market justice in education followed the expected pattern, providing evidence to support \(H_{3}\). Here, identification with the left aligns with the progressive tendencies that have typically characterized this group on various issues, such as reducing inequality, expanding social rights, and improving quality of life, for instance (Rivera, 2023). In contrast, groups that identify with the right in terms of political ideology tend to support market-based distribution criteria (Castillo, Iturra, et al., 2025; Lee & Stacey, 2024), and are less likely to align with criteria of equity and equality (Van Hootegem, 2022). Although this pattern of relationships is consistent with what has been previously found in the literature, a specific finding emerged when the interactions between the different latent profiles and political identification were examined: Congruent meritocrats who identify with the right exhibit a moderation in their rejection of market-based justice in education. This can be explained by the identity realignment currently taking place on the right; in the past, the right found a coherent discourse within a defined value system, whereas now some right-wing groups have distanced themselves from the mainstream, which is reflected in the fact that adherence to this political spectrum can coexist with supposedly contradictory conditions (Häusermann et al., 2026). Thus, within a latent group that rejects privilege, identification with the right acts as a catalyst for the legitimization of inequalities.
In summary, the results show that studying belief patterns using person-centered methods can provide new insights into how perceptions and preferences regarding merit and privilege are organized in people’s minds. Beyond that, this heterogeneity in people’s attitudinal makeup reveals that, by studying merit alongside privilege, we can observe that the relationship between merit and the legitimization of inequalities is not so straightforward. In this context, depending on which beliefs prevail among individuals, merit and privilege can either help to perpetuate or to reject the justification of inequalities in education. This “black box” containing meritocratic beliefs and the legitimization of inequalities has only just been opened; the interaction with political identification presents another finding that may yield new insights into the value systems that characterize the political spectrums of contemporary Chile.

title: 7  Conclusions
text:
This study has two limitations. First, there is a lack of information regarding the type of educational institution from which the respondents come. This information could have helped us refine our analysis of which types of people might be more or less willing to legitimize market-based criteria in education. Second, the scope of the study. To date, the multidimensional framework of meritocracy and privilege has been applied only in Chile, demonstrating that it can bring new perspectives to this research agenda. With this in mind, it is hoped that future studies will apply this multidimensional framework to new populations or even in cross-national comparative studies, thereby highlighting the role of beliefs about privilege in the study of market justice and opening the door to examining the contextual characteristics that may shape these relationships.
In addition to the future studies that may be undertaken, this paper seeks to contribute to the debate on educational justice within the context of a consolidated education market. By this, I mean revisiting concerns about the potential consequences of the commodification of education: normalizing market dynamics in a societal sphere such as education, without implementing the necessary safeguards for regulated operation, may end up further perpetuating existing inequalities. Although various policies have been implemented in Chile to address educational challenges such as discrimination and segregation (Ley General de Enseñanza, Ley de Inclusión Escolar, Gratuidad universitaria, for instance), it is necessary to establish forums that broaden the scope of the discussion and question the architecture of the Chilean educational system, along with the implications it has had and could have across various dimensions—namely, political, economic, and cultural. One element that can contribute to repositioning education in the national debate is understanding it as a matter of public concern. As Schinkel argues in the book of Camphuijsen et al. (2026), beyond being a public good, education must be understood as a concern at both the governmental and societal levels. His arguments call for treating education as a shared concern, given that there is a universal desire for everyone to receive a good education. In this vein, education constitutes a shared societal project, one that has the potential to shape individuals and mold the character of a society. Therefore, education should not be merely a collection of private interests; rather, it is urgent to restore its public character in alignment with the common good.

Table 5.3 reports the ordinal logistic regressions of market justice in education on the latent profiles. Congruent meritocrats are consistently less likely to endorse market justice in education than Partial meritocrats: the odds fall by 68% in the model with profiles only (OR = 0.32, 95% CI [0.26, 0.40]) and the association is virtually unchanged after adding sociodemographic controls (Model 2, OR = 0.31) and political identification (Model 3, OR = 0.35, p < .001). In contrast, Privilege advocates do not differ from Partial meritocrats in any model (OR between 0.93 and 1.00, p > .50), so the perception–preference configuration matters mainly through the meritocratic prevalence rather than through the endorsement of privilege.
Models 2 to 4 also adjust for sex (not shown in the table), and the estimates for the profiles are robust to this and to the other controls. Among the variables shown, university education is weakly and negatively associated with market justice (Model 2, OR = 0.82, p < .05; Model 3, OR = 0.84, p < .05). Income quintiles show no significant differences with respect to Q1 in any model. Political identification, introduced in Model 3, is also relevant: identifying with the left reduces the odds of supporting market justice by 38% compared to not identifying (Model 3, OR = 0.62, 95% CI [0.51, 0.76], p < .001; Model 4, OR = 0.62, p < .001), and identifying with the right increases them by 55% (Model 3, OR = 1.55, 95% CI [1.28, 1.87], p < .001); the center does not differ from the reference category (OR = 1.07 in Model 3, p > .05). Adding political identification improves model fit (AIC = 5,626 in Model 3 versus 5,694 in Model 2; BIC = 5,708 versus 5,758).
Model 4 tests whether the effect of the profiles varies among those who identify with the right. The interaction with Congruent meritocrats is positive and significant (OR = 1.71, 95% CI [1.07, 2.74], p = .026), whereas the one with Privilege advocates is not (OR = 1.26, p = .258). This means that the lower support for market justice among Congruent meritocrats is attenuated on the right: the main effect for this profile is OR = 0.30, but the combined odds ratio for right-wing Congruent meritocrats is about 0.52 (0.30 × 1.71), compared with Partial meritocrats who do not identify with the right. The interaction should be interpreted with caution, since it is only moderately significant and the interactions with the left, the center and university education (not shown in the table) were not significant.
